title: Letters on hearts (2 Corinthians 3:1–6)
hookLine: you are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit
tomorrow: why would a tentmaker call the human body a tent?

cards: First job application, and there's the box: references. Someone has to vouch for you. In Corinth, some visiting teachers seem to have arrived with letters like that.

Paul doesn't carry one. So he asks, a little dryly, "need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you?" Then he points at the people reading: "Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men."

teach.h: NOT WITH INK, BUT WITH THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: Anyone in Corinth can read that letter without opening a thing: just watch how these people live. And the author isn't Paul.
They are "the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart." Tables means tablets.
That picture belongs to Israel's prophets first: Jeremiah hears God promise, "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts."
Then Paul's hardest line: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." Christians have argued over it, and two readings stand out.
One, heard in Origen and others after him: the letter is the surface sense of scripture, the spirit its deeper meaning, and reading only the surface misses the life.
Its best case: Paul is talking about what's written and how it's read. The other is Augustine's: it isn't surface against depth.
A command known by heart, without grace to keep it, can only condemn; the Spirit gives the life to live it.

Its best case: Paul sets ink and stone against the Spirit writing on hearts, not plain meaning against hidden meaning. Neither reading makes the law the problem; Jeremiah's promise is the law written on hearts.
And both keep Paul's point: the letter he cares about most is a life.

how: Some churches still write a letter of transfer or commendation when a member moves to a new congregation; some preachers point to 2 Corinthians 3:2 to say a congregation's life is its real reference.

o: a prayer copied out by hand each morning
a thank-you note left for the next person
a life the Spirit writes, read by others

games.q: letters on hearts — tap the pairs.
p: but with the Spirit of the living God

s: 'the letter killeth' means Paul thought reading scripture closely was dangerous
Christians read it as surface and depth, or as command and grace; neither says stop reading.
the picture of God writing on hearts appears first in Israel's prophets
Jeremiah: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.
Paul carried a letter of recommendation to Corinth
he asks, need we, as some others, epistles of commendation? the church itself is his letter.

games.q: your friend reads 'the letter killeth' Augustine's way, as command without grace. you lean toward Origen's surface-and-depth reading. what's her best case?
o: Paul sets ink and stone against the Spirit writing on hearts, not plain against hidden.
Paul says all written scripture is dangerous and ought to be set aside.
Paul never mentions the Spirit anywhere in this part of the letter.
games.why: the Augustine reading leans on 3:3: not with ink, not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart. the Origen reading leans on how scripture is read. both keep Paul's point: a life is the letter.

practice: Write one line by hand, on paper if you can: something you'd hope a person reading your life this week would find there. Look at your handwriting for a moment, uneven and entirely yours.
Then fold it, and set it where you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: Letters on hearts. Paul's picture of a church as a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit, read in how people live.

orig.note: Greek: a letter; the King James renders it epistle in 2 Corinthians 3:2–3.

carryVoice: Your line: a living letter, written by the Spirit and read by everyone who knows you. Rest well.
